titles.Right lymphatic duct system: Right lymphatic duct and its trunks

Thoracic duct system.description: The thoracic duct is the body's main lymph channel. It collects lymph from the lower body and the left side of the head, neck, chest and arm, and returns it to the blood at the left venous angle.
clinical: If the thoracic duct is torn, for example during chest surgery, trauma or a tumour in the chest, chyle can leak into the pleural space. This is called a chylothorax.
Virchow node above the left collarbone
Tumour cells from the abdomen can travel up the thoracic duct to this node, so a hard, enlarged node above the left collarbone can be a warning sign of abdominal cancer.

Great veins.description: The internal jugular and subclavian veins join at each venous angle, where lymph returns to the blood. The two brachiocephalic veins unite to form the superior vena cava, which brings blood from the head, neck and arms to the heart; the inferior vena cava does the same for the lower body. The azygos and hemiazygos veins drain the posterior chest wall.
clinical: A tumour or clot that blocks the superior vena cava makes the face, neck and arms swell and dilates the veins over the chest wall. Lung cancer and lymphoma in the mediastinum are the classic causes.

Aorta and branches.description: The aorta is the main artery leaving the heart. It rises from the left ventricle, arches back over the root of the left lung and descends through the chest and abdomen. Its branches, including the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian and coeliac arteries, supply the head, neck, arms and abdominal organs.

Lymph nodes.description: Lymph nodes are small bean-shaped filters along the lymph vessels. Lymph passes through them, where immune cells can trap germs and cancer cells. The groups shown here are the main regional stations draining the neck, armpit, chest and abdomen.
clinical: Breast cancer often spreads first to the armpit (axillary) nodes, so these nodes are checked during breast cancer surgery, often by sentinel node biopsy. If many of them are removed, lymph from the arm can back up and cause lasting swelling (lymphoedema).
Cervical nodes often swell and feel tender during throat infections such as tonsillitis.

Viscera.description: The oesophagus (food tube) and trachea (windpipe) are shown as landmarks. The thoracic duct passes behind the oesophagus as it climbs through the chest, so the two lie very close together.
clinical: Surgery on the oesophagus can tear the thoracic duct, which runs close behind it, and cause a chylothorax.

Skeleton.description: The spine (cervical, thoracic and lumbar vertebrae) protects the spinal cord, and the thoracic duct and cisterna chyli lie in front of it. The clavicles (collarbones) lie close to the venous angles, where lymph enters the blood.

Diaphragm.description: The diaphragm is the dome-shaped skeletal muscle that separates the chest from the abdomen and drives breathing. The aorta and thoracic duct pass through it at the aortic hiatus, an opening near the spine.

parts.description: Intestinal trunk: usually a single vessel that collects lymph from the stomach, spleen, pancreas and most of the small and proximal large intestine, and carries it to the cisterna chyli. It is formed by vessels leaving the nodes around the coeliac and superior mesenteric arteries, and carries chyle, the milky, fat-rich lymph taken up by the lacteals (small lymph vessels) in the intestinal villi. It runs upwards behind the pancreas and joins the cisterna chyli in front of the first and second lumbar vertebrae.

Right lumbar trunk: a lymphatic vessel that runs up the front of the lumbar vertebrae beside the inferior vena cava and aorta, formed by efferent vessels from the right lumbar (lateral aortic) lymph nodes. It collects lymph from the right lower limb, the pelvic and abdominal walls, the pelvic organs and the right kidney, and carries it up to the cisterna chyli. The left lumbar trunk does the same on the other side, so lymph from both legs reaches the thoracic duct, not the right lymphatic duct.

Left lumbar trunk: a lymphatic vessel that runs up the front of the lumbar vertebrae on the left side of the aorta, formed by efferent vessels from the left lumbar (lateral aortic) lymph nodes. It collects lymph from the left lower limb, the pelvic and abdominal walls, the pelvic organs and the left kidney, and carries it up to the cisterna chyli. Together with the right lumbar trunk, it brings lymph from both legs to the cisterna chyli, where the thoracic duct begins.

Left jugular trunk: a lymphatic vessel that carries lymph from the left side of the head and neck, collected mainly by the deep cervical lymph nodes that lie along the internal jugular vein. It runs down the left side of the neck beside that vein and usually empties into the end of the thoracic duct at the left venous angle, where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet. It may instead open directly into the vein at that angle.

Left subclavian trunk: a lymphatic vessel that carries lymph from the left upper limb, collected by the axillary lymph nodes in the armpit, and from the upper chest wall and the left breast. It climbs from the armpit to the root of the neck beside the subclavian vessels, and usually joins the thoracic duct where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet. Most breast lymph passes through the axillary nodes first, so this trunk is one of the main routes by which it reaches the blood.

Left bronchomediastinal trunk: a lymphatic vessel that collects lymph from the left lung, the nodes around its bronchi, mediastinal organs such as the oesophagus and heart, and the deep wall of the left chest. It ascends through the superior mediastinum (the upper central chest between the lungs) and usually empties into the end of the thoracic duct where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet. It may instead open straight into the vein at that junction. The right bronchomediastinal trunk usually drains into the right lymphatic duct instead.

Right jugular trunk: a lymphatic vessel that carries lymph from the right side of the head and neck, collected mainly by the deep cervical lymph nodes along the right internal jugular vein. It runs down the right side of the neck beside that vein and usually empties into the right lymphatic duct at the right venous angle, where the right internal jugular and subclavian veins meet. The left jugular trunk, on the other side, usually empties into the thoracic duct instead.

Right subclavian trunk: a lymphatic vessel that carries lymph from the right upper limb, collected by the axillary lymph nodes in the armpit, and from the upper chest wall and the right breast. It climbs from the armpit to the root of the neck beside the subclavian vessels, and usually joins the right lymphatic duct where the right internal jugular and subclavian veins meet. Most breast lymph passes through the axillary nodes first, so this trunk is one of the main routes by which it reaches the blood.

Right bronchomediastinal trunk: a lymphatic vessel that collects lymph from the right lung, the nodes around its bronchi, mediastinal organs such as the oesophagus and heart, and the deep wall of the right chest. It ascends through the superior mediastinum (the upper central chest between the lungs) and usually empties into the right lymphatic duct where the right internal jugular and subclavian veins meet. It may instead open straight into the vein at that junction. The left bronchomediastinal trunk usually drains into the thoracic duct instead.

Internal jugular veins: large veins that drain the brain, face and neck, continuing from the sigmoid sinus through the jugular foramen at the base of the skull. Each runs down the neck inside the carotid sheath, lateral to the common carotid artery and deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and joins the subclavian vein behind the sternal end of the clavicle to form the brachiocephalic vein. In a neck dissection it is the large vein lying beside the common carotid artery, and that position is how to recognise it.

Left subclavian vein: the continuation of the axillary vein beyond the outer border of the first rib, carrying blood from the left upper limb. It runs medially under the clavicle, in front of the anterior scalene muscle, and joins the left internal jugular vein behind the sternoclavicular joint to form the left brachiocephalic vein. The subclavian artery lies behind the scalene muscle, so the vein is the vessel in front of it, and the left venous angle at the junction is where the thoracic duct usually empties.

Right subclavian vein: the continuation of the axillary vein beyond the outer border of the first rib, draining the right upper limb. It runs medially under the clavicle, in front of the anterior scalene muscle, and joins the right internal jugular vein behind the sternoclavicular joint to form the right brachiocephalic vein. The right lymphatic duct empties into this right venous angle, which is where lymph from the right head, neck, arm and chest returns to the blood.

Left brachiocephalic vein: formed behind the left sternoclavicular joint by the union of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins. It runs obliquely to the right across the front of the three large branches of the aortic arch, and joins the right brachiocephalic vein behind the upper sternum to form the superior vena cava. It is the longer of the two brachiocephalic veins, and its crossing of the midline above the aortic arch is what sets it apart.

Right brachiocephalic vein: a short, nearly vertical vein formed behind the right sternoclavicular joint by the union of the right internal jugular and right subclavian veins. It descends behind the upper sternum and the right first costal cartilage, and joins the left brachiocephalic vein to form the superior vena cava. As it does not cross the midline, its short, vertical course on the right side of the upper mediastinum identifies it.

Superior vena cava: the large, thin-walled vein that returns blood from the head, neck, arms and upper thorax to the right atrium of the heart. It is formed behind the right first costal cartilage by the two brachiocephalic veins, runs down the right side of the superior mediastinum beside the ascending aorta, and receives the azygos vein just before it enters the pericardium. It has no valves, and obstruction of it causes swelling of the face, neck and arms.

Inferior vena cava: the large vein that returns blood from the lower limbs, pelvis, abdomen and kidneys to the right atrium. It is formed at about L5 by the two common iliac veins, ascends on the right of the aorta, and passes through the diaphragm at about T8 to reach the right atrium. It receives the renal veins and, higher up, the hepatic veins, and in a dissection it is recognised by lying to the right of the aorta, behind the liver.

Azygos vein: the chief vein of the posterior chest wall, draining the back of the thorax together with the oesophagus and bronchi. It begins in the abdomen, rises through the diaphragm beside the aorta, lies on the right of the vertebral column, and arches over the root of the right lung at about T4 before entering the back of the superior vena cava. Because it links the abdominal and superior venae cavae, it is an important collateral route when the inferior vena cava is blocked.

Hemiazygos vein: a vein on the left of the vertebral column that drains the lower left posterior chest wall, together with the left bronchi and oesophagus. It ascends from the lower back, crosses behind the descending aorta and thoracic duct at about the level of T8, and joins the azygos vein on the right. On the left of the spine it is the counterpart of the azygos, and its course behind the aorta is what identifies it.

Ascending aorta: the short first part of the aorta, rising from the left ventricle upwards and to the right, behind the pulmonary trunk, until it reaches the sternal angle. The left and right coronary arteries arise from its root just above the aortic valve, so the first branches of the aorta feed the heart muscle itself. It is recognised as the thick-walled vessel leaving the heart and enclosed in the pericardium.

Aortic arch: the curved part of the aorta above the root of the lungs, running backwards and to the left from behind the sternal angle to about the level of T4. Three large branches leave its upper surface, the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, which supply the head, neck and arm. The ligamentum arteriosum, the remnant of the foetal ductus arteriosus, runs from its undersurface to the left pulmonary artery, and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks beneath it.

The thoracic aorta is the part of the aorta lying inside the chest. After the aortic arch it runs down the left side of the spine in the posterior mediastinum and passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at about T12 to become the abdominal aorta. Its branches include the posterior intercostal arteries to the chest wall and the bronchial and oesophageal arteries, and in a chest section it is the large round vessel against the front of the spine.

The abdominal aorta is the part of the aorta lying below the diaphragm. It passes through the aortic hiatus at about T12, runs down in front of the lumbar vertebrae just left of midline, and divides at about L4 into the two common iliac arteries. Its unpaired branches include the coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arteries, and its paired branches include the renal and gonadal arteries. The infrarenal segment, the part below the renal arteries, is the commonest site of abdominal aortic aneurysm.

The brachiocephalic trunk is the first branch of the aortic arch. It arises from the front of the arch, runs up and to the right behind the right sternoclavicular joint, and divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. It crosses in front of the trachea and supplies the right side of the head, neck and upper limb. On a dissection it is the first large branch to follow from the arch.

The left common carotid artery is the second branch of the aortic arch. Unlike the right common carotid, it arises directly from the arch rather than from the brachiocephalic trunk. It runs up to the left of the trachea into the neck, where it lies in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein and vagus nerve, and it divides at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage into the internal and external carotid arteries, which supply the brain, face and scalp.

The left subclavian artery is the third branch of the aortic arch, arising from its posterior part. It arches up and over the apex of the left lung into the root of the neck, runs between the scalene muscles over the first rib, and continues as the axillary artery. It supplies the left upper limb, and branches such as the vertebral and internal thoracic arteries arise from it.

The coeliac trunk is a short, unpaired branch of the front of the abdominal aorta, arising at about T12 just below the aortic hiatus. It runs forwards and divides into the left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries, which supply the stomach, upper duodenum, liver, spleen and pancreas. In a dissection it is the first single vessel to leave the front of the aorta, lying above the superior mesenteric artery.

The oesophagus is the muscular food tube that carries swallowed food from the pharynx to the stomach. It runs behind the trachea in the neck and then through the posterior mediastinum in front of the spine, and passes through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm at about T10. Its lining is non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, and in a section it appears as a collapsed tube with folded mucosa.

The trachea is the windpipe, a cartilage-supported airway that carries air from the larynx into the chest. It runs down the front of the oesophagus and divides at the carina, a ridge opposite the sternal angle at about T4 to T5, into the right and left main bronchi. Its wall has C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, open at the back, and its lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells.

The cervical vertebrae are the seven small vertebrae of the neck, numbered C1 to C7. Each of C1 to C6 has a transverse foramen, a hole in the transverse process that carries the vertebral artery and vein, and the spinous processes of C2 to C6 are split into two. The unforked spinous process of C7, the vertebra prominens, is easy to feel at the base of the neck and is the landmark for counting the other vertebrae.

The thoracic vertebrae are the twelve vertebrae of the mid-back, numbered T1 to T12, and each one forms joints with a pair of ribs. Their bodies and most of their transverse processes carry rib facets, and their long spinous processes slope steeply downwards, which helps tell them apart from the cervical and lumbar vertebrae. Together with the ribs and sternum, they form the bony wall of the chest.

The lumbar vertebrae are the five large vertebrae of the lower back, numbered L1 to L5, and they carry much of the body's weight. Their bodies are large and kidney-shaped, they have no rib facets, and their short, blunt spinous processes project straight backwards. The abdominal aorta and inferior vena cava lie in front of them, and the cisterna chyli, a lymph sac, lies in front of L1 and L2.

The clavicles are the two S-shaped collarbones that each connect the sternum to a shoulder blade. The medial end joins the manubrium of the sternum at the sternoclavicular joint, and the lateral end meets the acromion of the scapula. Lying just under the skin, the clavicle protects the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus beneath it. The venous angles, where lymph returns to the blood, lie just behind its medial end.

The deep cervical lymph nodes form a chain along the internal jugular vein, deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle in the side of the neck. They collect lymph from the head and neck, including from the superficial cervical nodes, and their efferent vessels join to form the jugular lymph trunk, which drains towards the venous angle. Their enlargement is a common sign of spread from head and neck cancers.

The lateral cervical lymph nodes are the group lying along the spinal accessory nerve in the posterior triangle of the neck, behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle. They drain the back of the neck and scalp, and their lymph passes on to the deep cervical chain. In a dissection, follow the spinal accessory nerve across the posterior triangle to find them.

The axillary lymph nodes are the nodes of the armpit, lying in the fat around the axillary vein and its branches. They drain the upper limb, the breast and the skin of the chest and abdominal wall above the umbilicus, and their vessels unite to form the subclavian trunk. They are a key site of spread from breast cancer.

The paratracheal lymph nodes lie in the superior mediastinum along both sides of the trachea. They receive lymph from the trachea, oesophagus and thyroid gland, and their vessels drain into the bronchomediastinal trunks. In a neck or upper chest dissection, they sit alongside the trachea rather than within its wall.

The tracheobronchial lymph nodes lie around the lower trachea, the carina (the ridge where the trachea divides) and the main bronchi, close to the roots of the lungs. They drain the lungs and airways, and their vessels pass on to the bronchomediastinal trunks. Enlargement of these nodes is a key feature in staging lung cancer.

The pre-aortic lymph nodes lie in front of the abdominal aorta, around the origins of the coeliac and superior mesenteric arteries. They drain the stomach, duodenum, pancreas, spleen, liver and intestines, and their efferent vessels form the intestinal trunk, which carries lymph to the cisterna chyli. In a dissection they are found in the fat at the front of the aorta, behind the pancreas.

The lateral aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes lie in a chain along the sides of the abdominal aorta, in front of the lumbar vertebrae and behind the peritoneum. They drain the lower limbs, pelvis, kidneys, gonads and posterior abdominal wall, and their efferent vessels form the lumbar trunks, which usually join the cisterna chyli. They are the usual first site of spread from testicular cancer.

The intermediate lumbar lymph nodes lie between the aorta and the inferior vena cava, in front of the lumbar vertebrae. They drain the lower limbs, pelvis, kidneys and gonads, and their vessels join the lumbar trunks. In a retroperitoneal dissection they sit in the fat between the two great vessels.

The left lumbar lymph nodes are the lumbar nodes lying on the left side of the abdominal aorta, in the retroperitoneal fat in front of the left lumbar spine. They drain the left kidney, left gonad and left lower limb, and their vessels form the left lumbar trunk, which usually joins the cisterna chyli. On the left, they carry lymph from the leg towards the thoracic duct.
